title: Writing is no longer proof of work
content:
Tech companies structurally depend on writing to serve as evidence, in the same way that Bitcoin depends on proof-of-work hashing. However, in the last few years, LLMs have started to undermine this practice.

How can writing be like proof-of-work? When I’m writing something at work, it’s not always to communicate an idea. Sometimes it’s because having a piece of writing is useful as evidence: of compliance with some process, of the fact that I put in effort, or of the fact that I know about some topic. Here are some examples.

Writing as evidence of compliance

The most obvious instance of writing as evidence is filling out mandatory templates: “risk assessments”, “impact evaluations”, and so on. The purpose of these is rarely to assess risk or evaluate impact. It’s some combination of:

  • Employees wanting to demonstrate that they’re taking some incident seriously by introducing new process
  • A legal requirement that companies have developed the least-expensive way to technically satisfy
  • Internal company rules intending to scare lazy or uncommitted engineers away from making dangerous changes
  • Smaller companies trying to role-play processes from larger companies that are doing one of the above

It’s a mistake to buckle down and produce an excellent piece of writing here. You simply need to dash off something plausible enough to tick the box.

Writing as evidence of effort

In the kinds of hundred-page reports produced by consultants, writing is evidence of effort. The actual piece of communication is the first page of text (or often not even that). The remaining ninety-nine pages are proof that the first page is well-researched, and that the money spent on hiring the consultancy wasn’t wasted.

Another example: if you’re working on a project by yourself, why spend time creating tickets and filling them out? I suppose theoretically someone could read them to get a sense of what you’re doing, but in that case you’ve failed to communicate the project via normal channels: telling people in Slack or in meetings, writing a proposal document, and so on. The tickets are primarily valuable as evidence: proof1 that you haven’t just been screwing around playing video games.

Writing as evidence of learning

A third subcategory of writing-as-evidence is writing that proves that the writer has understood some topic.

The best example of this is reporting. Large organizations function via a tree of nested reports, often called “rollups”. Individual contributors give status updates to their managers, who summarize and combine those into team-level updates for their managers, and so on all the way to the top.

One of the reasons for this practice is that it forces each manager to build at least a minimal mental model of what’s going on in their local area. Taking the time to write a status report forces you to wrap your head around each detail, for the same reason that the best way to understand an idea is to try to explain it to someone else. Even if the VP or CEO doesn’t read the rollup, the fact that it exists is evidence that the manager has some grip over their domain.

Proof of work

You can think of all these kinds of writing-as-evidence as proof of work. Nobody really cares about the content, they care about the fact that you sat down and wrote it. Of course, this requires a measure of trust. Just like cryptocurrency proof-of-work, if you fake it (for instance, by pasting lorem ipsum into pages 2-100 of your report), you can swindle the rewards without having to actually put in the effort.

To avoid fraud, tech companies will typically check some percentage of writing-as-evidence: either reactively, such as when an incident causes people to actually go and read the risk assessment on the PR that broke production, or proactively, by tasking some poor soul with reviewing the consultant report in detail. Blockchains, of course, are able to check the work automatically (for instance, by confirming that the nonce and block data do in fact hash to the claimed value).

To break Bitcoin, somebody would have to break SHA-256: to figure out a way to identify in advance what content would hash to a specific value, so you could produce the hash without doing the work. To break writing-as-evidence, somebody would have to figure out a way to generate text on demand, so you could produce the evidence (of compliance, effort or learning) without actually doing the work. Unfortunately, that happened in 2023.

LLMs fundamentally break writing-as-evidence

Writing is no longer evidence of anything. LLM-produced writing makes evidence of compliance even more vacuous than it already is. It totally destroys evidence of effort: if you need a hundred-page report, you can generate one with an hour and a few dollars in inference tokens. Evidence of learning is likewise broken, since I can produce a detailed status report full of information that never passed through my mind at all (and certainly was never retained).

Of course, this problem isn’t limited to tech companies. Schools and universities rely on writing to serve as evidence of effort and learning, and students are using LLMs to cheat as hard as they can. Many political or regulatory bodies require a certain bar of professional writing in order to filter requests, and are or will be overloaded by LLMs making that kind of writing generally available.

What happens now?

Currently we’re suffering through an overhang period where the processes are still in place but everyone knows how to trivially exploit them. It will be interesting to see how organizations adapt. They might:

  • Introduce new, harder-to-forge forms of evidence like recording a video or presenting live in a meeting (though this will take more time to consume than written reports)
  • Attempt to mandate that certain forms of writing not be AI-generated (universities already do this2), which will be difficult to enforce
  • Find other ways to track effort, such as asking an LLM to review an engineer’s code and judge how much work they put in

I can’t think of any great options here, which is interesting. If there really is no easy solution to this problem, the overhang period might go on for a while, where nobody is particularly happy with the status quo but there are no good alternatives.

In this scenario, individual software engineers are incentivized to exploit the system while they can, and avoid being harmed by other system-exploiters. In other words: don’t trust or waste time poring through LLM-authored documents yourself, but also don’t waste time writing documents by hand that are just intended to serve as evidence3. Save that effort for documents that are intended to serve as communication.

  1. Why not just look at your code? Code is an illegible metric to non-technical people. Even to technical people it can be tricky to figure out how difficult a piece of code was to write, for the same reason that it’s tricky to assess how difficult a mechanical puzzle is just by seeing it when it’s assembled. But everyone knows roughly how long it takes to write a paragraph of text.

    ↩

  2. Software companies will be reluctant to adopt this, because they see internal LLM adoption as a necessary tool to speed product development. They’re already begging employees to use LLMs; if they start telling them to not use LLMs for writing, that muddies the message.

    ↩

  3. Part of this involves getting good at telling the difference (in other words, getting good at figuring out if anyone is actually going to read the document). There may also be a third emerging category here: texts that won’t be read but also won’t be ignored, because they’re intended for consumption by other LLMs.

    ↩

title: ★ HomeView Thoughts and Observations
content:
I’ll start with a nomenclatural sidenote: Apple seems to be going with “Apple HomeView” as the product’s name. E.g., the URL slug for it on Apple.com is apple-homeview/, not just homeview/. Few people notice and no one who doesn’t work in Apple product marketing cares, but they actually do the same thing with Vision Pro — in Cupertino, it’s “Apple Vision Pro” (once again including the URL slug). Yet this week’s new HomePod Mini is just “HomePod mini 2” and the existing 2nd-generation HomePod is just “HomePod (2nd generation)” — not “HomePod 2” or “Apple HomePod”. I certainly intend to just call it “HomeView”.

Apple introduced HomeView with a three-minute introductory film simulating a suburban family’s hectic before-school/work kitchen rush hour, with versions hosted on Apple’s site and YouTube. The most ridiculous aspect of it is that anyone would possibly make their kid French toast in that scenario. I’d have told my son to make his own goddamn French toast with that attitude. Or I’d have made a single serving and eaten it myself right in front of him. Bro.

I do think the basic concept is an intriguing idea. But as an implementation of that concept, my initial impressions are threefold. First, I am unconvinced that anyone in a family would use this for anything other than playing music or podcasts, rather than just using their phones. And if that’s the case, why not just have a HomePod? Apple’s video shows family members taking turns to use the HomeView, rotating it on the kitchen island to face themselves. Why? Why does the mom check her calendar on this, rather than on her iPhone, while the dad is using it to follow a French toast recipe? There’s a real “Why do we need this?” question here and I don’t think Apple’s video answers it, at all. You need to think you want it if you’re going to buy it. And even if you already had a HomeView set up, I’m not sure how often you’d use it instead of your phone, or instead of just talking to it like a screenless HomePod.

Second, all the touching and rotating — in Apple’s own demonstration — makes it seem awkward that HomeView must be tethered to a USB power cable. If you look closely in the video, they do show the USB power cable in some shots, but not many. And if you look really closely, this hypothetical family has drilled a hole in the center of their kitchen island to snake the cable through.

The hero shot introducing the product, of course, does not show the power cable at all:

We see a wee bit of the cable when the dad reaches to touch the screen to start the French toast recipe:

And then a few seconds later, after the mom rotates the HomeView to the side, so she can check her calendar (despite the fact that she knows the dad was using it to follow a recipe), we get our most honest shot of the cabling situation:

The above shot is at 0:49. It’s followed by two quick cuts to the dad and then the younger daughter, then at 0:52 we cut back to the mom (curious about her daughter’s new boyfriend situation), and, lo, the shot is now framed in such a way that we no longer see where the cable goes:

If you think that slight reframing is happenstance, you should stay away from poker tables. Most kitchen islands I’m familiar with — including my own — have power outlets on the sides of the island. I’m sure some people have power outlets on the top surface of the counter, but I can’t recall seeing one. These are kitchen counters, not office desks. But either way, there’d be a long USB-C cable cluttering the countertop. And if you do happen to have a power outlet on the top surface of your counter, there’d be an adapter sticking out of it, all the time, to duplicate this HomeView setup.

This family’s convenient hole in the center of their island countertop is a fantasy. Where does the cable go underneath? How exactly do they have a power adapter plugged in down there? What happens when something spills on the counter? When we custom ordered our kitchen, we weren’t asked if we wanted any holes drilled in our island countertop, and if we had been asked, it would have made me wonder if the guy asking the question had a hole or two drilled in his head.

I know, it’s a marketing video. Marketing videos present products in ideal settings. But the power cable is an essential aspect of the standalone HomeView. I’m not suggesting that it should be battery powered. You’d still need to plug it in every few days, which would mean most people would just leave it plugged in, which gets us back to needing to live with an always-visible cable and power adapter in one of our living spaces. The countertop hole this cable disappears into in this video is less ideal and more dishonest.

The wall-mounted option seems more appealing to me, but now you’re talking about a home improvement project and (for most of us) calling an electrician. And that raises the question of why the wall-mounted version costs the same $300 as the one with the connected base, even though the base provides the subwoofer. And it requires a mount, and the mounts cost $60 (USB-C), $80 (AC wired), or $130 (PoE — and this one is not available yet). So the wall-mounted version, when you include a mount, costs more but sounds worse? This doesn’t make sense.

Those points make me skeptical that there’s a place for HomeView in my home. We have a stereo pair of HomePods in our kitchen. Neither is on the center island, because that would be dumb. They’re on the counters along the outside of the kitchen, each near an outlet on the wall. In the four days since HomeView was announced, I’ve tried to imagine when I’d want to look at something on a screen on either of them. My count remains at zero.

My third early impression is that the display is surprisingly small. I saw HomeView in person in New York on Tuesday, and I think Apple’s video conveys its size very accurately. It’s small and cute. It’s much more like a HomePod Mini with a screen than a full-size HomePod with a screen. For some reason I was expecting the latter. This is not a complaint, simply an observation. I actually think that making it small and cute makes it about as unobtrusive as an ever-present screen could possibly be. That’s good. But because it’s small you need to be close to it to read anything more detailed than large glanceable widgets.

The major difference between a device with a screen and one without is that you can watch video on a device with a screen. But HomeView clearly isn’t intended for that. It can play video but isn’t primarily meant to play video. If it were it would have a widescreen aspect ratio. But instead it has a square aspect ratio,1 which is decidedly unsuited to video, unless, I suppose, you want a screen that is equally unsuited for both widescreen and tallscreen video.

So my skepticism boils down to the question of why anyone would want to add one (or more!) additional ever-present screens to our homes and lives. Phones can stay in our pockets until we need them. Watches remain on our wrists. HomePods can be tucked away unobtrusively in corners, and remain fully useful. HomeView needs to be in a prominent location for its display to serve any practical purpose. Apple’s initial pitch for it doesn’t earn that prominence for me.

  1. In my thoughts and observations column after Apple’s iPhone event last month, I wrote the following regarding the iPhone Duo’s clever 1:1.4 aspect ratio:

    Here’s the thing. If you take a 2 : 1 or even 2.2 : 1 aspect ratio phone display and turn that into a book-like foldable, the inner screen comes out square — or so close to square that we might as well just call it square. Nobody makes any device of any sort that just has a square display. Square is a terrible aspect ratio for a phone or a tablet or a laptop or a desktop display. The only square displays on the market are the inner displays for Android foldables from the last decade. Square being a shitty aspect ratio is half the reason almost no one has bought those things.

    I will admit that I had the as-yet-unannounced HomeView in mind as I wrote that, given that its square aspect ratio had been rumored for months. HomeView is not a phone or tablet or laptop or desktop display. It’s not a TV either. So maybe square works for this nascent product category (status boards?). But if square does prove to be correct for this purpose, it’ll be the first category I can think of where that’s true. Apple Watch is the closest device I can think of whose screen serves primarily to display status, but even Apple Watch isn’t square. (It varies slightly by model, but Apple Watch displays are around 4 : 5.) ↩︎

And even if you already had a HomeView set up, I’m not sure how often you’d use it instead of your phone, or instead of just talking to it like a screenless HomePod.

title: Cloud of suspicion lifted from NIST curves
content:
NIST published a set of elliptic curves for cryptography in 2000. The seeds for the curves were supplied by the NSA, and cryptographers suspected the agency may have installed backdoors in the curves. And not without reason: the NSA did insert a backdoor in the Dual_EC_DRBG random number generator.

Two days ago researchers at Anthropic [1] showed that the NIST curves were not seeded with a backdoor. The rest of this post will give the background necessary to appreciate this result.

The security of elliptic curve cryptography depends on the difficult of solving the discrete logarithm problem. In the context of elliptic curve arithmetic, the analog of exponentiation is easy but the analog of taking logarithms is hard.

In general it’s not practical to compute discrete logarithms over large elliptic curves. But it could be easy for someone with inside information to compute discrete logarithms if something about the curve was not “general.”

Specifically, the NIST curves have the form

y² = x³ − 3x + b (mod p)

for various values of p [2], and the suspicion regards the choice of b. For nearly all values of b encryption over the elliptic curve should be secure, as far as we know, but in principle someone could engineer values of b to weaken the encryption.

So where did the b‘s come from? Were they chosen in good faith?

Concern over the choice of seeds, the b‘s, grew following the Snowden revelations. Daniel J. Bernstein emailed Jerry Solinas of the NSA on September 6, 2014 asking where the seeds had come from. Solinas replied in subsequent emails. He said the seeds were generated by hashing the ASCII representation of a humorous English message, but he could no longer remember the exact message or the precise hashing procedure.

On October 5, 2023 Philippo Valsorda announced a bounty for reverse engineering the origin of the NIST elliptic curve seeds. Two days ago researchers from Anthropic claimed the bounty. Valsorda verified the results and awarded the prize. It turns out Solinas found the curve seeds in good faith, but his memory had faded over the years since the curves were published. We now know he used a date, not a phrase, as part of the process of constructing the seeds.

The NIST curves have some nice properties, such as enabling some clever tricks for arithmetic in their base fields. But adoption of the curves has been held back over suspicion regarding their origin. Now the curves have been exhonorated. As Valdorda notes

… this nicely completes the “rehabilitation arc” of NIST elliptic curve cryptography, which I would now personally recommend over Curve25519/Ed25519/X25519. Just in time for them to be retired in favor of post-quantum signatures.

Related posts

  • What is an elliptic curve?
  • Monero’s elliptic curve
  • Lewis Carroll and zero knowledge proofs

[1] This does not imply that LLMs are necessarily a threat to encryption. The search for the NIST seeds required a lot of brute force. Some cleverness was required in order to come up with possibilities to check by brute force, but even that is sorta brute force at a higher level of abstraction. There has been speculation that labs are looking for weaknesses in cryptographic primitives and protocols, but that’s a different matter than searching for seeds.

[2] The curves P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 are built over the field of integers mod p, where the number of bits in p corresponds to the number in the name. The P-192 curve, for example, has as its base field the integers mod 2192 − 264 − 1, a 192-bit prime.
